newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh identified as man who rented bomb truck.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh identified as man who rented bomb truck.

text.p: The owner of a rental agency on Friday identified Timothy McVeigh as the man who rented the truck used to blow up the Oklahoma City federal building as the prosecution continued to rapidly build its case.

Eldon Elliott, of Elliott's Body Shop in Junction City, Kansas, told McVeigh's trial that the 29-year-old Gulf War veteran rented the truck under the name of Robert Kling and presented a South Dakota driver's license in that name.
"That's him, the man in the blue shirt," Elliott said, pointing to McVeigh in the courtroom.
The prosecution's case has been speeding along since testimony started two weeks ago and the government is now expected to wind up its case in the next two weeks.

Elliott's testimony was the first time that a witness had directly identified McVeigh as having rented the truck that authorities say was used to blow up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
An axle from the destroyed truck was one of the first major pieces of evidence recovered after the bombing and a hidden identification number on it led authorities to the Junction City rental agency.

The prosecution contends tht McVeigh is Kling and that he drove the 20-foot (six metre) truck full of explosives to Oklahoma City about five hours away. McVeigh has pleaded not guilty. He faces the death penalty, if convicted.
Elliott said the renter came to his shop on Saturday, April 15, saying he wanted a truck to drive to Nebraska from Kansas and wanted to pick it up the following Monday afternoon.

Elliott added that McVeigh declined to take insurance on the truck even though the rental agency owner warned him that he would be liable for any damage. Elliott quoted McVeigh as saying, "I won't need it ... I'm a good driver." McVeigh paid $280.32 for the rental, including an $80 deposit, the rental agent said.

Elliott testified that McVeigh did not go outside with him for the customary walk around inspection of the vehicle when he came back to the rental office to pick the truck up on Monday, April 17, 1995.
Elliott also testified that he saw another man standing in the corner of the rental office while McVeigh was there, but could not identify him. "I just barely glanced at him as I walked outside."

Initially, investigators believed two men rented the truck, a weakness the defence tried to exploit during cross- examination. But Elliott held firm, saying he did not know who the second man was although he did see him talk to McVeigh.
The man was originally believed to be a suspect dubbed by officials as John Doe No. 2. A nationwide manhunt was launched, but failed to turn up a second suspect.
The day of the bombing, Elliott received a call from the Ryder headquarters in Florida, notifying him that the truck he had rented out was believed to be the one used to carry the explosives.

Elliott testified that he told FBI agents the man who rented the truck was about 5 foot 10 inches (1.7 metres) to 5 foot 11 inches (1.8 metres), with a medium build and short hair. But under cross examination he admitted he was not really certain of McVeigh's height.
Also, on the stand Elliott said he could not remember what the man wore, despite earlier statements he made saying the man may have been clad in military-style clothing.
The clothes are important because a video security tape from a nearby McDonald's restaurant taken about 15 to 20 minutes before McVeigh picked up the truck showed him in civilian clothes.

Elliott said an FBI agent asked him if the man wore military clothes. "I said it could be because 75 percent of our customers are military," Elliott said. But he insisted on the stand that he paid no attention to what McVeigh was wearing.
Chief defence counsel Stephen Jones demanded to know why it took Elliott 48 days to identify McVeigh, but Elliott insisted he knew who he saw even if he was a bit slow in making a final judgment.
Elliott also insisted he had not tailored his testimony to qualify for a $2 million reward. "I even signed a letter saying there wasn't going to be any reward," he said.
The owner of a Chinese take-out restaurant said she had food delivered to a man named Kling at a local motel. The food was taken to the room that McVeigh had rented under his own name.
